content: To improve access to palliative care, it is essential to educate policymakers, healthcare workers, and the public while implementing palliative care services aligned with the principles of universal health coverage. A sustainable, high-quality, and accessible palliative care system must be integrated into primary healthcare, community, and home-based care. This system should also support caregivers, including family members and community volunteers. While specialist palliative care is a critical component, all healthcare providers should be trained in pain management and addressing the needs of patients with life-threatening illnesses. Providing palliative care is an ethical obligation for healthcare professionals. Developing a palliative care policy can take various forms, such as a standalone policy, part of a national health plan, or an element of strategies for non-communicable diseases (NCDs), HIV/AIDS, or cancer control. When planning a palliative care policy, it is crucial to involve relevant partners, such as the Ministry of Health, other government ministries, healthcare workers, professional organizations, NGOs, academic institutions, ethics committees, and funding bodies. International partners, including the WHO, UN agencies, and international NGOs, should also be considered. For example, Malawi’s national palliative care policy, approved in 2014, integrates equity, access to pain medicines, capacity-building, resource allocation, patient and family participation, coordination, referral systems, education, communication, care for children, and research. The policy outlines implementation arrangements at all levels of the healthcare system and provides a monitoring and evaluation framework. Since its adoption, Malawi has achieved significant milestones, including estimating national palliative care needs, establishing reporting mechanisms, ensuring government coverage of 58% of palliative care services, enabling local reconstitution of morphine powder into oral morphine, making morphine available in government and faith-based health units, and training over 300 palliative care trainers. Planning a palliative care policy should begin with a thorough assessment of the current situation and population needs. This includes evaluating the availability and coverage of existing services, the availability of essential palliative care medicines (e.g., oral morphine), and estimating the quantitative and qualitative needs for palliative care. Strategies for scaling up and integrating palliative care into the healthcare system should be based on these assessments, with a focus on areas of greatest need and existing resources. A stepwise approach to introducing palliative care programs can be used, covering policy actions, healthcare financing, service delivery, workforce development, access to medicines, and information and research. Improving access to pain relief and palliative care medicines requires addressing barriers at various levels, including regulatory, legislative, knowledge, and systemic issues. For instance, restrictive regulations on opioid prescribing, lack of training for healthcare providers, societal fears about opioids, and financial disincentives in healthcare systems can all limit access. Strategies to overcome these barriers include regulatory reforms, embedding palliative care in healthcare training curricula, raising public awareness, and integrating palliative care into primary healthcare and universal health coverage packages. WHO has published guidelines to help governments eliminate unnecessary barriers to accessing controlled medicines and has developed tools to address prescribing, supply chain, and cost barriers. National essential medicines lists should include palliative care medicines, such as opioids for pain relief, and these lists should be widely available and linked to clinical guidelines. Once essential palliative care medicines are added to a country’s essential medicines list, additional steps are needed to achieve full clinical access. These include obtaining approval from the health ministry to register the medicine, ensuring importation and distribution, negotiating contracts and pricing, and formally registering the medicine in the country. Efforts should also focus on ensuring affordability, preventing stock-outs, and addressing any resistance from regulatory or policing authorities.
